title: Jason Boehmig, CEO of Ironclad on Balancing Risk, Innovation, and AI Opportunity in the Legal Field
author: Jason Boehmig

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Boehmig supports the move from ad hoc lawyer assistance toward repeatable, workflow-based contract delivery and materially extends the cluster by specifying an incumbent-vendor strategy: embed AI selectively in established workflows, generate structured data, preserve model flexibility and address enterprise data trust. His evidence is experiential and qualitative, so it does not establish wider organisational transformation or ROI.

st.t: Startup scaling: Founder context can become bottleneck
st.an: Boehmig accepts founder-led risk-taking and customer-informed product development, while materially extending the cluster’s balancing proposition with a clear boundary: experimentation should not transfer company risk to customers. Rigorous testing and a high release threshold operationalise that customer-protection principle, though he does not address delegation or founder-context bottlenecks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Boehmig accepts the cluster’s view that enterprise legal-AI value depends on institutional absorption rather than features alone, and materially extends it by identifying buyer sophistication, data governance, contractual protections, an existing enterprise footprint and shared architecture as concrete adoption mechanisms. His separation of core execution from incubation also adds an operating-model approach for balancing deployment and experimentation.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Boehmig supports the cluster’s proposition that dependable legal AI requires task-specific orchestration rather than reliance on a single model or generic capability. His multi-model strategy and distinction between case-law citation reliability and contract-lifecycle needs reinforce the synthesis’s account of task-dependent model selection, though he provides strategic examples rather than comparative performance evidence.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: Boehmig supports the cluster’s incumbent-adaptation account by advocating product-by-product AI integration into an existing scaled CLM platform wherever it creates user value. The source presents incremental embedding as one route forward but offers no comparative evidence that it outperforms replacement or ground-up rebuilding.

st.t: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
st.an: Ironclad supports the cluster’s proposition that legal-AI value comes from product-level integration of domain expertise rather than generic task acceleration. Its task-specific model selection, use of AI across CLM where it creates user value, and focus on contract-language performance and proprietary data align with bounded, context-specific workflows. The source offers strategic expectations rather than measured evidence of reliability or durable advantage.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Boehmig supports the cluster’s workflow-layer thesis by advocating product-specific AI deployment, model selection by legal task, and combinations of improving foundation models, retrieval and legal datasets rather than reliance on an isolated specialist model. His emphasis on defined customer value and accumulated attorney trust also aligns with the cluster’s adoption and workflow-fit claims, though he provides little direct evidence about human verification or professional accountability.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: Boehmig supports the cluster’s account of AI reshaping vendor strategy: Ironclad embeds AI where it creates product-specific value, pursues new products despite cannibalisation risk, and locates differentiation in specialised legal applications rather than foundational models. The source does not address the cluster’s central caveat about slower integration, migration and adoption constraints.

kp.k: Workflow automation addresses repetitive corporate legal work
kp.d: Boehmig describes standardising incorporation and financing documents and automating document comparisons as the origins of Ironclad. His account identifies repetitive document production and coordination, rather than replacement of legal judgment, as initial automation targets. He reports counting 17 clicks for a document-comparison operation repeated across 20–30 redlines; this is personal workflow experience, not a systematic productivity study.
qs: how can we standardize the practice of law how can we automate some parts of it

I actually one time counted the number of clicks that it would take me to take one word file compare it with another word file and output a PDF that was named the way I wanted to was like 17  clicks and sometimes you're doing 20 30 red lines

kp.k: Contract reliability drove a shift toward structured workflows
kp.d: Boehmig says Ironclad moved from an email-based assistant concept to workflows because even a hypothetical 5% error frequency was unacceptable in business contracts. He presents 100% accuracy as the requirement and workflows as the way to achieve it, without providing measured accuracy evidence. Workflows also produce structured contract data, linking contract creation to subsequent management.
qs: what we realized was workflows were a better way of making contracts than just a AI That's on an email Alias
even if that AI would get  something wrong 5% of the time you really can't have that in a business contract
we had to be like 100% um accurate
once you have a workflow at at the end of that workflow you have a bunch of really great structured data

kp.k: AI extends contract management through large-scale data extraction
kp.d: Boehmig dates consideration of transformer-based opportunities to around 2018, initially targeting extraction rather than wholesale automation of legal services. He describes extracting data from 10,000 PDFs into an existing database as a potential source of customer value. The figure illustrates the intended use case, not a reported evaluation sample or demonstrated deployment result.
qs: 2018 we started saying okay there's there's a potential breakthrough here it's not necessarily usable yet
if we can get the ability to extract from 10,000 PDFs all of the data and put them in our database as well that's going to generate a ton of value for our customers
we started retooling  with the idea of layering in AI specific Al at that point into just the data extraction

kp.k: Established user trust may support lawyers' AI adoption
kp.d: Boehmig reports that Ironclad's attorney users are receptive to AI, contrary to the general narrative he perceives. He attributes part of this difference to trust developed over 10 years, which enables dialogue and experimentation with users. This is a vendor's interpretation of its own customer experience, not evidence that all lawyers are similarly receptive.
qs: we do find that attorneys are pretty amenable to AI which I think like it kind of runs contrary to the popular narrative
we've definitely done a lot over the past 10 years to win attorney Trust
that accounts for kind of like some of the Delta between what we see in our user base and what like the General Industry sees

kp.k: Corporate experimentation is distinguished from customer-facing risk
kp.d: Boehmig endorses substantial company-level risk-taking but says customers should not bear product risk. He describes rigorous testing and a high release threshold for a standalone AI-native product, explaining its delayed launch as deliberate caution. These are stated operating principles, not demonstrated guarantees of risk-free use.
qs: I would just distinguish between like um risk tolerance that we have as a company and risk tolerance that we have like to put an experience in front of our customers
I'm comfortable taking a lot of risk
I don't want my customers to be taking any risk in using the product
you could say we've been slow to launch that I would say we've been we have a really  high bar for what we're gonna put our name behind

kp.k: Embedded AI supports incumbent growth and product learning
kp.d: Boehmig says embedding AI throughout an established contract lifecycle management product generates user feedback and ideas for new products. He identifies first-draft AI review and extraction as natural CLM applications and attributes growth and improving quarterly unit economics partly to embedded AI. No financial breakdown or causal analysis is supplied.
qs: it's let us get a bunch of data back from users around like what they like like where they see the value and it's also led to the ideation of new products for us
CLM is this natural place to put a lot of AI whether it's that first draft AI review or the data extraction
the unit economics of the business are improving quarter over quarter
the AI goodness uh from layering that into our existing product has accounted for that

kp.k: Incumbents should incubate potentially cannibalising AI products
kp.d: Boehmig recommends retaining the direction of the core product while placing separate incubation bets, judged by different criteria. He invokes Geoffrey Moore's organisational-zone framework and argues that successful new AI products could cannibalise Ironclad's existing line. Cannibalisation is a prospective strategic risk, not a reported outcome.
qs: I really do think we have to disrupt ourselves
it could cannibalize our existing product line if it's really successful
you can't lose the direction of your main product
you can have like an incubation Zone which is where you're trying out new ideas and those can be judged on totally different things

kp.k: Competitive advantage lies in vertical applications, not foundation models
kp.d: Boehmig locates proprietary investment in legal applications while favouring continued access to state-of-the-art foundation models. He reports using OpenAI, Google and Anthropic rather than committing exclusively to one provider, because negotiation, summarisation and bulk extraction require different capabilities. He frames superior contract-language understanding and recommendations, supported by distinctive data and viewpoints, as a prospective 10-year advantage.
qs: the verticalized application stuff is things that we're going to need to be uniquely good at and we're going to develop our own proprietary stuff around
we're not all in on any one of them
it's everything from like a commercial contract negotiation to summarization of like 270 pages of m&a docs to extracting data from 10,000 contracts
understanding and recommending contract language um that's like where we feel like the 10year sustainable Advantage is

kp.k: Rapid model advances can undermine custom-model strategies
kp.d: Boehmig argues that a custom-model approach attractive nine months earlier could leave a product stuck on GPT-3 and forgo later foundation-model improvements. Using case-law accuracy as an example that he says is more relevant to general legal AI than CLM, he claims newer models, retrieval-augmented generation and better datasets produce superior results. His statements about eliminating or reducing hallucinations are qualitative assertions without benchmark results, error rates or evaluation methods.
qs: the problem with that is that model stuck on gpt3 and it doesn't have GPT 4 it doesn't have GPT 40 you lose all of the benefits of the main branch
the hallucination level is so much less on GPT 4 than it was on gpt3
application of rag that help you supplement and make sure that you're not hallucinating the case law
a much better result than the approach from 9 months ago of kind of forking the model

kp.k: Custom-model marketing may diverge from technical performance
kp.d: Boehmig says completely custom-trained legal models have an appealing marketing story even where he believes staying with advancing foundation models delivers better results. He considers market recognition of this distinction incomplete. The host separately suggests that custom-model narratives can also appeal to investors; that investor claim is not presented as Boehmig's evidence.
qs: I do think there's a marketing message which is we have an llm that's completely custom trained for you that  does land
I think the market is still playing catchup to the reality of the results
that's taking some time to come out

kp.k: Enterprise adoption depends on data governance and buyer confidence
kp.d: Boehmig attributes enterprise adoption barriers more to buyer understanding and discomfort about data use than missing features. He says Ironclad's provider contracts prohibit using customer data for foundation-model training and storage by those providers. He regards contractual protections and an existing trusted architecture as adoption advantages; these are vendor-reported arrangements, not independently reviewed findings.
qs: I think it's less about features and it's more about sophistication of buyers and getting them comfortable with a new ways of thinking about data
we have zero training contracts with all of our providers such that our customers data is not being used to train any foundational model and isn't even getting stored there
it's more of an addendum to the existing work they've done than a net new process

kp.k: Enterprise trust creates an incumbent advantage over young vendors
kp.d: Boehmig argues that early-stage vendors struggle to reassure enterprise legal teams because of limited history, funding and sophistication in explaining data handling. He contrasts that with Ironclad's established corporate presence and predicts greater comfort as vendors mature and industry standards emerge. His categorical statement about Series A startups is an opinion, not a documented market-wide finding.
qs: particularly in Enterprise there's just no chance of a series a  startup getting the legal team comfortable
they just haven't been around a long enough
more companies will mature it will get more comfortable there's going to be more of an industry standard

kp.k: Replacement and adoption statistics originate in the host's framing
kp.d: The host contrasts AI-enhanced workflows with products marketed as replacing paralegals or general counsel and expresses doubt that the technology is ready for the latter. The host also attributes single-digit legal production adoption to a report identified in the transcript as 'Bane' and says enterprise production adoption fell year over year. No report title, sample or methodology is supplied; Boehmig responds through product strategy and data-governance arguments rather than independently substantiating these statistics or endorsing wholesale replacement.
qs: it's going to completely automate away your need for a paralal or a general counsel which like I don't think the technology is ready for that yet
Enterprise adoption of AI has actually gone down year-over-year when you look at applications that have made it into production
according to this report that Bane put out especially in the legal profession when you look at adoption in production is still like single digits

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Boehmig presents AI as a means of improving contract workflows, extracting contract data and recommending language, with adoption dependent on reliability, trust and data protection. He also predicts competitive advantages from specialised applications rather than isolated foundational models.
pts.d: Jason Boehmig makes seven linked claims. (1) Contract creation cannot tolerate the illustrative error rate of an email-based AI assistant; structured workflows were Ironclad's route to what he describes as 100% accuracy, while also producing structured data. AI extraction can bring data from large collections of existing PDF contracts into the same database and generate customer value. (2) Lawyers are more amenable to AI than the popular narrative suggests, particularly where a provider has already earned their trust. (3) Embedding AI in an established contract lifecycle management (CLM) product—for drafting, review and extraction—has delivered business benefits to Ironclad, including growth and improving unit economics. User feedback from that deployment also informs new products. (4) Current foundational models, supplemented by customisation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and improved legal datasets, produce better results than the earlier approach he describes as forking a model for legal data. He says GPT-4 hallucinates less than GPT-3 and describes RAG as helping prevent fabricated case law. (5) He locates Ironclad's potential ten-year competitive advantage in superior understanding and recommendation of contract language, supported by proprietary viewpoints and data, rather than any particular technical implementation. (6) Enterprise legal-AI adoption is constrained less by missing features than by buyers' discomfort about data use and protection. Established vendors can introduce AI on existing architecture and contractual relationships more readily than early-stage startups can secure legal-team confidence. He expects company maturation, greater comfort and industry standards to improve this situation. (7) New AI products could cannibalise Ironclad's existing product line, but he considers taking that risk necessary. These are claims about a legal-technology vendor and its corporate customers, not claims that Ironclad delivers legal work as an ALSP. Boehmig does not independently assert the host's suggested tenfold productivity gain or complete replacement of paralegals and general counsel.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Boehmig's experience as a lawyer, founder and vendor executive, supplemented by descriptions of product deployment, internal testing and technical changes; no quantified evaluation results are supplied.
pts.d: For workflow reliability and contract-data value, Boehmig recounts Ironclad's transition from a manually operated email service to structured workflows and later AI extraction. The 5% error rate is an illustrative unacceptable scenario, not a reported measurement; the asserted 100% workflow accuracy is not accompanied by a validation study. His claim about lawyers' receptiveness rests explicitly on Ironclad's own user base and its accumulated customer trust. For business benefits, he reports growth and quarter-over-quarter improvements in unit economics, attributing benefits to AI integration, without supplying figures or a causal comparison. For model strategy, he describes internal experience, continuing assessment of OpenAI, Google and Anthropic models, RAG, and an improved Harvard case-law database. He expresses strong satisfaction with results but gives no named benchmark, test protocol, hallucination rate or published head-to-head comparison. His claims about adoption draw on enterprise customer experience and contractual safeguards, including provider agreements that he says prohibit training on or storing customer data. The proposed ten-year advantage and future adoption improvements are strategic expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes. The host's references to a Bain report, single-digit production adoption and declining enterprise adoption are not findings independently presented by Boehmig.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview combines current deployment claims, a retrospective account of rapidly changing model strategy, and longer-term competitive and adoption predictions whose timing is mostly unspecified.
pts.d: In the supplied 2024 source, Boehmig says Ironclad began seriously considering transformer-based extraction around 2018–2019, before he regarded the technology as necessarily usable. His present-tense claims concern AI already embedded in CLM and a standalone AI product still undergoing rigorous testing. He contrasts the model-customisation strategy he considered best approximately nine months earlier with newer foundational models, RAG and datasets available at interview time; this is a contingent claim about a fast-changing technical environment, not a timeless preference against customisation. His projected sustainable advantage in contract-language understanding has an explicit ten-year horizon. Wider enterprise adoption has no specified deadline: it depends on vendor maturity, confidence in data handling and the emergence of standards. Receptiveness to AI is qualified by prior vendor trust, and the adoption advantage he describes applies particularly to enterprises and existing customer relationships. Reliable contract creation is a product requirement in his account, not a demonstration that every AI-generated legal output is error-free. He expressly distinguishes case-law accuracy, which he says is less relevant to CLM, from the requirements of a more general legal-AI product. Cannibalisation remains conditional on new products' success and is acknowledged as difficult to predict.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal teams and contract users, established legal-software vendors, and competing AI startups; the source does not forecast profession-wide employment losses or access-to-justice gains.
pts.d: Corporate lawyers and enterprise legal teams are users and buyers of tools for making contracts, reviewing drafts, recommending language, summarising lengthy transaction documents and extracting information from contract portfolios. Corporate customers benefit, in Boehmig's account, from structured data and integrated AI but require protection against incorrect contract information and unwanted data reuse. Existing Ironclad customers can adopt AI as an extension of an established product and security review rather than through a wholly new procurement process. Ironclad and other incumbent vendors can gain product feedback, growth and operating benefits from integration, while exposing themselves to potential cannibalisation from new AI products. Early-stage legal-AI vendors face a trust and procurement disadvantage in his enterprise-market account. Providers that isolate themselves on older customised models risk missing foundational-model improvements; application providers can instead differentiate through contract expertise, data and task-specific model selection. The account is primarily one of software-supported legal work, not a substantiated prediction of autonomous lawyer replacement, altered law-firm staffing, lower legal fees or improved access to justice.
